title: Celonis case study: object-centric process mining

cards.question: Which three problems does the Celonis presentation give as reasons why organizations lack a holistic understanding of how they run?
cards.answer: Systems are disconnected, departments have different objectives, and teams operate in silos.
distractors: Event logs are too large, models are too complex, and tools are too expensive.
Processes are too simple, data is too clean, and managers are too busy.
Customers are unhappy, suppliers are late, and regulations are changing.

cards.question: Why do different executives (CFO, COO, CCO, CIO) make a holistic process view difficult?
cards.answer: Each has different objectives, such as reducing operating costs (CFO), increasing reliability and productivity (COO), increasing revenue and customer experience (CCO) and modernizing with AI (CIO).
distractors: Each uses a different process mining algorithm.
Each owns a different event log format.
Each is responsible for a single case.

cards.question: The presentation says processes are hard to see and harder to improve because there are three different views of a process. What are they?
cards.answer: How the process was designed, how businesses think the process runs, and how the process actually runs.
distractors: Control flow, data and resources.
Discovery, conformance and enhancement.
Case, event and trace.

cards.question: What is the difference between how a process was designed and how it actually runs?
cards.answer: The designed process is the intended model; the actual process is what happens in practice and can be seen from event data.
distractors: The designed process is the log; the actual process is the model.
The designed process has noise; the actual process does not.
They are always identical for audited processes.

cards.question: Which process areas are listed as examples of interconnected business processes?
cards.answer: For example Order Management, Quote-to-Cash, Procurement, Accounts Payable, Hire-to-Retire and Record-to-Report.
distractors: Only Accounts Payable.
Only manufacturing processes.
Only IT processes.

cards.question: Give examples of hidden value in processes mentioned for Supply & Distribution.
cards.answer: 1 in 5 orders cancelled due to stock-outs, more than 70% of orders expedited, and more than 8 delivery date changes for the same order.
distractors: Invoices paid twice and goods shipped but not billed only.
Service ticket reassignments only.
Missing sustainability coverage of suppliers only.

cards.question: Give examples of hidden value in Finance & Administration processes mentioned in the presentation.
cards.answer: Invoices paid twice, goods shipped but not billed, and more than 10 service ticket reassignments.
distractors: 1 in 5 orders cancelled due to stock-outs.
20% of truck shipments can be consolidated.
No sustainability coverage of suppliers.

cards.question: What sustainability opportunities are mentioned as hidden value?
cards.answer: 20% of truck shipments can be consolidated, and there is no sustainability coverage of suppliers.
distractors: Invoices paid twice.
8 delivery date changes for the same order.
800,000 returned products not accounted for only.

cards.question: How is process mining defined in the presentation, with reference to van der Aalst?
cards.answer: A data analytics technology to reconstruct, analyze and improve business processes, analysing how processes actually work in practice and uncovering insights into performance and compliance challenges.
distractors: A technology to design new business processes without data.
A statistical method to predict customer behavior.
A technique to convert source code into process models.

cards.question: What are the three building blocks of Object-Centric Process Mining (OCPM)?
cards.answer: Objects, events and relationships.
distractors: Cases, activities and timestamps.
Places, transitions and tokens.
Nodes, edges and weights.

cards.question: What are objects in OCPM?
cards.answer: Digital representations of tangible items that flow through a process, such as customer, sales order and invoice.
distractors: Activities that happen to the process.
Links between events.
Rules of the process model.

cards.question: What are events in OCPM?
cards.answer: All activities that happen to objects, such as creating a user account, packing an order or sending an invoice.
distractors: Customers and invoices.
Connections between orders and deliveries.
Process variants.

cards.question: What are relationships in OCPM?
cards.answer: How objects connect to one another, for example one order can have many deliveries and one invoice can have many orders.
distractors: The sequence in which events occur within a case only.
The list of resources performing events.
The mapping of events to IT systems.

cards.question: What is the limitation of traditional (case-centric) process mining according to the presentation?
cards.answer: It can only reflect events that are directly linked to the single case running through a specific process.
distractors: It can only handle processes with fewer than 10 activities.
It requires an event log without timestamps.
It cannot discover control-flow models.

cards.question: What does OCPM enable that traditional process mining does not?
cards.answer: It connects all objects and events across enterprise operations, enabling true end-to-end analyses.
distractors: It removes the need for event data.
It guarantees sound models.
It only analyses single departments.

cards.question: What is the difference between case-centric and object-centric process mining?
cards.answer: Case-centric mining follows one case notion, with each event belonging to one case; object-centric mining lets an event relate to multiple objects of different types, capturing interconnected processes.
distractors: Case-centric mining uses Petri nets; object-centric mining uses process trees.
Case-centric mining is for conformance; object-centric mining is for discovery.
They differ only in the file format of the log.

cards.question: Why can a single event relate to several objects in OCPM but not usually in classical event logs?
cards.answer: Classical logs assign each event to exactly one case id, whereas OCPM stores events and their relationships to many objects (e.g. an order and an invoice).
distractors: Classical logs do not use timestamps.
OCPM events have no activity names.
OCPM logs have no objects.

cards.question: Why can case-centric mining cause problems when one order has many deliveries and one invoice covers many orders?
cards.answer: Choosing one case notion forces a flattening of the data, which duplicates events or loses relations, so the view of the end-to-end process is distorted.
distractors: Such relations are not allowed in ERP systems.
It makes the log too small.
It introduces no problems.

cards.question: In the automotive analogy, what does a case-centric view tell you about a finished car?
cards.answer: What happened: the sequence of steps such as engine assembly, body assembly, paint job and final assembly.
distractors: Which plant produced a specific engine.
Whether the exhaust filtration unit was verified after final fitment.
When the seat was delivered.

cards.question: In the automotive analogy, what kind of questions does the object-centric view answer?
cards.answer: Why and how questions about the objects involved, such as which plant produced a specific engine, when a seat was delivered, or whether the exhaust unit was verified after fitment.
distractors: Only how many cars were produced.
Only the order of assembly steps.
Only the cost of each car.

cards.question: Which layers does the Celonis Platform diagram list for data?
cards.answer: Data sources (structured, semi-structured and unstructured), data infrastructure, data core and context model.
distractors: Cases, events and traces.
Model, log and diagnostics.
Extract, load and display.

cards.question: What is at the center of the Celonis Platform diagram?
cards.answer: The Process Intelligence Graph, combining process data and business knowledge.
distractors: A Petri net.
A single event log.
A dependency graph of resources.

cards.question: What activities does the platform diagram connect around process intelligence?
cards.answer: Design, analyze and operate, with AI-driven processes combining humans, AI agents and automations.
distractors: Discover, check and repair.
Extract, transform and load.
Plan, execute and close.

cards.question: Which companies are the case studies of this year?
cards.answer: Nykredit and Novo (Novo Nordisk), plus a case with a teaching assistant.
distractors: Maersk and Carlsberg.
LEGO and Vestas.
Siemens and SAP.

cards.question: What is Nykredit, and which subprocess is the focus of its case?
cards.answer: Denmark's leading mortgage lender; the case focuses on the mortgage lending process, in particular property valuation.
distractors: A drug developer; the focus is clinical trials.
A logistics company; the focus is shipment planning.
A telecom provider; the focus is customer churn.

cards.question: What does Nykredit want to achieve with process mining?
cards.answer: Improve efficiency and customer experience in mortgage lending while remaining compliant, and understand how performance differs across customer segments, property types and regions.
distractors: Reduce clinical trial duration.
Consolidate truck shipments.
Replace all manual staff with AI.

cards.question: Which processes are the focus of the Novo Nordisk case?
cards.answer: Issue Management (IM) and Protocol Deviations (PD) in clinical trials.
distractors: Property valuation and credit assessment.
Quote-to-cash and procurement.
Hire-to-retire and record-to-report.

cards.question: Why are Issue Management and Protocol Deviations well suited for object-centric process mining?
cards.answer: The processes are closely related and originate from the same underlying data source, so their interaction can be analysed with objects and relationships.
distractors: They are both fully sequential processes.
They have no event data.
They are logged by two unrelated systems.

cards.question: What does Novo Nordisk want to learn about IM and PD cases?
cards.answer: How they move through the process, where delays or rework occur, how the two processes interact, and which improvements enable faster resolution, stronger compliance and better oversight.
distractors: Which patients should receive which drug.
How to predict drug sales.
How to discover a Petri net.

cards.question: What is the purpose of the case study's Proof of Value?
cards.answer: To convince C-level to invest in Celonis Process Intelligence, by mining ERP data and creating a value case.
distractors: To prove that the event log is complete.
To prove that the model is sound.
To train students on Petri nets.

cards.question: What are the stages of the process mining journey shown in the case study (Now … Spread Success)?
cards.answer: Extract, transform, analyse (the Proof of Value), then optimise & monitor and spread success (implementation).
distractors: Plan, build, test and deploy.
Discover, check, enhance and predict.
Collect, label, train and evaluate.

cards.question: Which stages belong to the Proof of Value, and which to the implementation?
cards.answer: Extract, transform and analyse belong to the Proof of Value; optimise & monitor and spread success belong to the implementation.
distractors: Extract belongs to the implementation; the rest to the Proof of Value.
All stages belong to the Proof of Value.
Spread success belongs to the Proof of Value.

cards.question: Research question 1 asks about process discovery and bottleneck identification. What does it ask?
cards.answer: How the actual end-to-end process deviates from the designed process, and which activities or handovers are the biggest bottlenecks for strategic KPIs.
distractors: How the data quality affects the process.
How to compare units on benchmarks.
How to compute financial impact.

cards.question: Research question 2 is about root cause analysis. What does it ask?
cards.answer: Which drivers, process patterns and data characteristics lead to frequent undesired activities or rework loops, and what is their quantifiable impact on cycle time, costs or compliance.
distractors: How the actual process deviates from the design.
How KPIs vary across dimensions.
How to benchmark best performers.

cards.question: Research question 3 concerns initial data quality. What does it ask?
cards.answer: To what extent the completeness and accuracy of master data correlate with downstream process efficiency.
distractors: Whether the event log has noise.
Which units are the best performers.
What the financial impact of rework is.

cards.question: Research question 4 concerns comparative performance and benchmarking. What does it ask?
cards.answer: How KPIs vary across different dimensions, and which process behaviors characterize the highest-performing units that can be standardized as best practices.
distractors: Which master data fields are missing.
Which activity is a bottleneck.
How the log was extracted.

cards.question: Research question 5 concerns analysis of inefficiencies. What does it ask?
cards.answer: Which combination of factors or process steps correlates most strongly with inefficiencies, and what their financial impact is.
distractors: How the actual process deviates from the designed process.
How data quality correlates with efficiency.
Which department has the most staff.

cards.question: What is the difference between research question 2 (root cause analysis) and question 5 (analysis of inefficiencies)?
cards.answer: Question 2 looks for drivers and patterns behind undesired activities or rework and their impact; question 5 finds the factor combinations most correlated with inefficiency and quantifies the financial impact.
distractors: Question 2 is about conformance; question 5 is about discovery.
Question 2 is about data quality; question 5 about benchmarking.
They are identical.

cards.question: Which deliverables are required in the case study?
cards.answer: Upload the data, build an object-centric data model, build the analysis in Celonis, prepare the value case, and give a presentation of about 5 minutes plus 5 minutes Q&A.
distractors: Write a thesis and submit it.
Build a Petri net by hand.
Implement a discovery algorithm in Python.

cards.question: What should the analysis focus on in the value case?
cards.answer: What to improve and how much this will save the company, with clear directions or solutions; value is key.
distractors: Only describing the process as it is.
Only the technical details of the data model.
Only the number of events.

cards.question: How long does the case study run, and how is it supported?
cards.answer: Over about 2 months, supported by Academy course material with step-by-step guidance and 3 Q&A sessions with the company's subject matter expert.
distractors: Over 1 week, supported by one lecture.
Over 6 months, supported by weekly exams.
Over 2 days, supported by a hackathon.

cards.question: When are the three Q&A sessions with the company SME?
cards.answer: October 19th, November 2nd–3rd, and November 24th.
distractors: September 1st, October 1st and December 1st.
October 5th, November 5th and December 5th.
Every Monday in October.

cards.question: What are the first steps students should take to start the case study?
cards.answer: Create an academic Celonis account with their academic email (selecting 'Student'), form a student group, and explore the Academy course material.
distractors: Install ProM and Disco.
Write the final presentation first.
Wait for the first Q&A session.

cards.question: Which topics does the recommended course material cover under ETL enablement?
cards.answer: Data integration basics, extract data, transform data and load data.
distractors: Introduction to Petri nets.
Process Adherence Manager.
Building a value case.

cards.question: Which topics does the recommended technical enablement cover?
cards.answer: OCPM in Action (building object-centric data models) and visualizing processes in a view.
distractors: Extracting data.
Building target models in PAM.
Introduction to process mining only.

cards.question: What does the Process Adherence course material cover?
cards.answer: The Process Adherence Manager (PAM): discovering it, event types, analyzing deviations, building a target model, and exploring deviating variants.
distractors: Extract, transform and load.
Building data models.
The Celonis academic alliance.

cards.question: What does a target model in the Process Adherence Manager represent?
cards.answer: The intended process against which actual behavior (deviating variants) is compared, supporting conformance analysis.
distractors: A prediction of future cases.
An aggregated event log.
A model of data sources.

cards.question: Why is the Process Adherence Manager relevant to the Nykredit and Novo cases?
cards.answer: Both cases involve regulated processes where compliance and deviations (such as protocol deviations) matter, which is analysed by comparing actual behavior with a target model.
distractors: Because it is needed to extract the data.
Because it replaces the object-centric data model.
Because it is required to build a presentation.

cards.question: Which analysts' recognitions are cited for Celonis in the presentation?
cards.answer: Leader in the Gartner Magic Quadrant for Process Mining Platforms 2025, the Forrester Wave for Process Intelligence Software 2025, and the Everest Group PEAK Matrix for Process Mining 2025.
distractors: Winner of the Turing Award.
Top ranked university for process mining.
Leader in only one analyst report.

cards.question: How does the 2026 Gartner Magic Quadrant name the category in which Celonis is a Leader?
cards.answer: Process Intelligence Platforms (formerly process mining).
distractors: Business Intelligence Platforms.
Robotic Process Automation Platforms.
Data Warehouse Platforms.
